sections.heading: How it works
sections.html:
You send the clothes washed or not; I press and stabilize every cut, so worn spots survive the machine. Before anything is sewn you receive a photograph of the layout, and nothing is final until you approve it.

Quilts finish six to eight weeks after approval, machine quilted, bound by hand, and shipped with the leftover scraps folded on top, labeled. The label gets names and dates in your own words.

items.q: How many shirts do I need?
items.a: Twelve for a throw, more for bigger quilts. Ties, collars, and pockets all count, and jeans can back the whole quilt.

items.q: The clothes are fragile. Is that a problem?
items.a: No. Every piece is fused to a lightweight stabilizer before it is cut, so worn thin places stitch down and stay down.

items.q: Can I keep one garment out of the quilt?
items.a: Of course. Tell me which pieces are off limits and they will go back in the box untouched.

sections.html: Every quilt here was photographed with its family's permission, and the stories behind them stay with the families. If your quilt appears and you would rather it did not, one message removes it.

sections.heading: The studio
sections.html:
I sewed professionally for a decade before the first memory quilt, and the difference is the pace. These quilts are waited for, so there is no assembly line here: one quilt at a time, laid out on the long table, photographed, and approved before a seam is sewn.

The studio is a converted sunroom with good light and a gate at the door for the dog. Visitors are welcome by appointment, and every family gets progress photos, whether or not they asked.

items.quote: She asked what my mother's curtains meant to us before she cut anything. That question is the whole difference.
items.author: L., spring client
